claim:handoff-units-and-binning.proposition: Each side alone, and the particle-to-grid handoff
claim:handoff-units-and-binning.hypothesis:
The FV process reproduces continuum diffusion to discretization accuracy. Smoldyn's binned
particle variance grows as 2Dt per axis. Binning conserves molecules exactly. Uniformly
distributed particles give a uniform binned concentration up to and including the
boundary nodes, because boundary elements have 1/2 (edge) or 1/4 (corner) volume as in
VCell's CartesianMesh.

provenance.note: Second order in space and first order in time; expected error ~1e-3 on this grid.
Free Brownian motion; 80,000 molecule samples give ~0.5% sampling error on the variance.
Every molecule maps to exactly one node (clamped nearest-node index).
Binomial sampling; |z| < 4 for a correct volume convention (corner 1/4, edge 1/2).

claim:field-modulated-decay.proposition: Field-to-particle coupling, A_particle -> 0 at rate k·[B](x)
claim:field-modulated-decay.hypothesis:
With a static field and immobile particles, each grid column survives as exp(-k·B·t)
exactly in expectation, and nothing decays where B = 0. With diffusing A and B, the
ensemble-mean particle concentration matches the all-continuous FV solution of the same
model, to within sampling noise.

provenance.note: Smoldyn's first-order reaction probability per step is 1-exp(-rate·dt), so survival is exp(-k·B·t) exactly in expectation.
Rate k·0 = 0 at the B = 0 nodes.
Per-node sampling noise of the 8-run mean is about 1/sqrt(8·165), roughly 2.8%; the threshold allows about 2x that.
Same exact expectation as the co-simulation test; validates the headless native reference path.
Equal expected survival under both solvers; 8 runs each.
Same model, mesh and coupling scheme in both solvers; differences only from sampling (8 runs each).

claim:two-way-exchange.proposition: Mass balance across the particle ↔ field handoff
claim:two-way-exchange.hypothesis:
Each side applies only its own half of each mixed reaction, so A + B is conserved in
expectation up to the O(dt) lag of the explicit coupling, and total A / total B → k2 / k1.
Field-dependent creation must use each grid node's actual cell volume (1/2–1/8 at
boundaries); otherwise creation is overproduced by Σ(full cells)/Σ(actual cells).

provenance.note: Conserved in expectation; the residual comes from the explicit-coupling lag plus the ~2-step creation start-up artifact.
Detailed balance of A ⇌ B; 16 seeds.
Exact expectation k2·[B]·V·602.214·t; the lower slack covers the ~2-step start-up artifact.

claim:bimolecular-hybrid.proposition: A_particle + B_field → C_field: two-way nonlinear coupling, both solvers
claim:bimolecular-hybrid.hypothesis:
The particle side removes A at rate k·[B](x), and the PDE side removes k·[A_binned]·[B]
from B and adds it to C. With 20,000 A, both solvers' ensemble means approach the
continuum solution (A treated as a field). The solvers differ only by sampling.
B + C is conserved exactly (PDE side).

provenance.note: Same model, mesh and coupling; independent ensembles of 16.
C is produced on the PDE side from binned A; any timing or units mismatch shows up here first.
20,000 molecules per run; the remainder is explicit-coupling lag plus discreteness.

claim:coupling-interval-convergence.proposition: Coupling error vs Smoldyn step multiplier, co-simulation (two schemes) and native VCell
claim:coupling-interval-convergence.hypothesis:
Explicit lagged coupling is first order in k·Δt. The co-sim "fvsolver" mode applies the
same lag as the embedded solver, so it has the same error. "start-of-interval" reads
the field at the start of the Smoldyn step instead of at T+(k−1)Δt, so its error
differs; its sign and size are to be measured.

provenance.note: Explicit lagged operator splitting is first order in the coupling interval.
Same scheme (SimTool.cpp main loop).
Same lag semantics (verified in tests/test_scheduling_semantics.py), so the same coupling error.

claim:performance-scaling.proposition: Wall time of the co-simulation vs the native VCell hybrid, with breakdown
claim:performance-scaling.hypothesis:
The co-simulation pays a per-step framework overhead (scheduling, state updates and
data marshaling between processes) that matters most for small problems. For large
problems, PDE and particle work dominate in both implementations.

provenance.note: A two-process composite should cost no more than a few milliseconds per step to schedule and marshal.

narrative.question: Can a process-bigraph co-simulation of a PDE process and a Smoldyn process reproduce the hybrid PDE/particle solver embedded in vcell-fvsolver to within its stochastic error, and at what computational cost?
